title: When expanding volume during mount make sure that node_stage is always set
body:
### What happened?

When a pod is quickly deleted and re-created on a node, it may not be necessary to unstage the volume and in which case only node-publish is called for the volume.

When this happens - stage_path won't be set for `NodeExpandVolume` RPC call because volume was *not* staged even though, volume does have `NODE_STAGE_UNSTAGE` capability. 

We should try and fix this behaviour so that - node_stage_path is always set in `NodeExpandVolume` RPC call. 

### What did you expect to happen?

We should try and fix this behaviour so that - node_stage_path is always set in `NodeExpandVolume` RPC call.

title: structured-merge-diff supports only  'set' type for associative list
body:
### What happened?

kube-apiserver has has this kind of entries in log
```
E0126 00:39:45.253562       1 fieldmanager.go:210] "[SHOULD NOT HAPPEN] failed to update managedFields" err="failed to convert new object (default/test-inline-claim; /v1, Kind=Pod) to smd typed: .spec.containers[name=\"with-resource\"].resources.claims: element 0: associative list without keys has an element that's a map type" VersionKind="/, Kind=" namespace="default" name="test-inline-claim"
E0126 00:39:46.700727       1 fieldmanager.go:210] "[SHOULD NOT HAPPEN] failed to update managedFields" err="failed to convert new object (default/test-inline-claim-resource; resource.k8s.io/v1alpha1, Kind=ResourceClaim) to smd typed: .status.reservedFor: element 0: associative list without keys has an element that's a map type" VersionKind="/, Kind=" namespace="default" name="test-inline-claim-resource"
```

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected those lines not to appear in kube-apiserver logs, and structured-merge-diff to support map types, like the comment says at https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/vendor/sigs.k8s.io/structured-merge-diff/v4/typed/helpers.go#L233

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

I ran into it during Dynamic Resource Allocation usage. It requires a either a CRI-O v1.23, or containerd 1.7+ (has to be built from git at the moment); the cluster has to be initialized "DynamicResourceAllocation" feature-gate and alpha apis enabled, for instance with this config for kubeadm :
<details>

```YAML

kind: ClusterConfiguration
kubernetesVersion: v1.26.0
imageRepository: registry.local
apiServer:
  extraArgs:
    feature-gates: "DynamicResourceAllocation=true"
    runtime-config: "api/alpha=true"
controllerManager:
  extraArgs:
    feature-gates: "DynamicResourceAllocation=true"
scheduler:
  extraArgs:
    "feature-gates": "DynamicResourceAllocation=true"
---
apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: KubeletConfiguration

  DynamicResourceAllocation: true
---
apiVersion: kubeadm.k8s.io/v1beta3
kind: InitConfiguration
nodeRegistration:
  criSocket: "unix:///var/run/crio/crio.sock"
---
apiVersion: kubeproxy.config.k8s.io/v1alpha1
kind: KubeProxyConfiguration
featureGates:
  DynamicResourceAllocation: true
```

</details>

Deploy pod with inline resource-claim for instance the following (the issue will appear immediately even though the resource-claim is malformed. Proper resource claim would require resource-driver to be deployed, but it's not necessary for issue to be manifested):
<details>

```YAML
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1alpha1
kind: ResourceClaimTemplate
metadata:
  name: test-inline-claim-template
  namespace: default
spec:
  metadata:
    labels:
      app: inline-resource
  spec:
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: test-inline-claim
spec:
  restartPolicy: Never
  containers:
  - name: with-resource
    image: registry.k8s.io/e2e-test-images/busybox:1.29-2
    command: ["sh", "-c", "ls -la /dev/dri/ && sleep 30"]
    resources:
      claims:
      - name: resource

nodes.title: dynamic resource allocation: avoid apiserver complaint about list content
nodes.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

This fixes the following warning (error?) in the apiserver:

    E0126 18:10:38.665239   16370 fieldmanager.go:210] "[SHOULD NOT HAPPEN] failed to update managedFields" err="failed to convert new object (test/claim-84; resource.k8s.io/v1alpha1, Kind=ResourceClaim) to smd typed: .status.reservedFor: element 0: associative list without keys has an element that's a map type" VersionKind="/, Kind=" namespace="test" name="claim-84"

The root cause is the same as in e50e8a0c919c0e02dc9a0ffaebb685d5348027b4: nothing in Kubernetes outright complains about a list of items where the item type is comparable in Go, but not a simple type. This nonetheless isn't supposed to be done in the API and can causes problems elsewhere.

For the ReservedFor field, everything seems to work okay except for the warning. However, it's better to follow conventions and use a map. This is possible in this case because UID is guaranteed to be a unique key.

#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:
Fixes #115330

#### Special notes for your reviewer:



#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?
```release-note
A fix in the resource.k8s.io/v1alpha1/ResourceClaim API avoids harmless (?) ".status.reservedFor: element 0: associative list without keys has an element that's a map type" errors in the apiserver. Validation now rejects the incorrect reuse of the same UID in different entries.
```

nodes.title: Fix panic on ClusterIP allocation for /28 subnets
nodes.body:
The ClusterIP allocator tries to reserve on part of the ServiceCIDR to allocate static IPs to the Services.

The heuristic of the allocator to obtain the offset was taking into account the whole range size, not the IPs available in the range, the subnet address and the broadcast address for IPv4 are not available.

This caused that for CIDRs with 16 hosts, /28 for IPv4 and /124 for IPv6, the offset calculated was higher than the max number of available addresses on the allocator, causing this to panic.

/kind bug
/kind regression
Fixes #115316

```release-note
Fix a regression in 1.25+ default configurations related to the ServiceIPStaticSubrange feature that caused the API server to panic when trying to allocate a Service with a dynamic ClusterIP and it has been configured with Service CIDRs with a /28 mask for IPv4 and a /124 mask for IPv6
```

title: Deletecollection failing after 34 seconds
body:
### What happened?

In a cluster with large enough numbers of objects, it seems to be impossible to clean them up with `deletecollection`.  Because the deletecollection is failing while listing the objects from etcd.  The failure happens after exactly 34 seconds, due to the 34-second max timeout introduced in PR #96901 (cc @tkashem for insight on that PR).



### What did you expect to happen?

The deletecollection should be able to run for longer, and succeed.

I recognise that there are still risks of the API server using too much RAM, if deleting a very large collection due to issue #90743.  But, until _that_ issue is fixed, it seems like allowing `deletecollection` to run for longer might be a good idea.  As far as I can tell, the 34 second timeout does not apply to normal LIST calls, so on that basis I feel it should not apply to the giant unchunked LIST call that happens inside `deletecollection`.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a few hundred thousand objects of some particular type.  (Argo workflowtaskresults happen to be the type I'm looking at while I write this)
2. Call deletecollection. (Optionally passing some kind of fieldSelector, but I don't think that's essential)
3. Observe that a 504 failure code is logged in kube-audit logs, and that a log entry similar to this is logged by the API Server `"List etcd3" key:<some key>,...,limit:0 ... (total time: 34000ms)`  (In practice, the total time may be a little over 34000 ms).
4. As far as I can tell, the delete collection really has failed at this point.  I notice that PR #96901 says that, in general, "The go-routine can keep running, while the timeout logic will return a timeout to the client" but I don't _think_ that's what's happening here.  I think that, because the 34 sec timeout is used in the context of the etcd call, the etcd list call really does fail, and so the code never proceeds to actually deleting anything.



### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

1.22

/cc

@JohnRusk  the `34s` deadline has been in effect before PR https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/96901 was introduced

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/9787f46bbf05349ca53cd8b04cd2f7a76771646a/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/endpoints/handlers/delete.go#L181-L184

If we remove this `34s` deadline from here, then the deletecollection request will have at most `60s` to complete (default).  
The list call that is failing in your case, is a direct call to the storage, right? 
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/9787f46bbf05349ca53cd8b04cd2f7a76771646a/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/registry/generic/registry/store.go#L1142-L1145

on the contrary, we don't enforce the `34s` timeout for LIST 
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/9787f46bbf05349ca53cd8b04cd2f7a76771646a/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/endpoints/handlers/get.go#L166

thinking out loud here:
- I don't know if it makes sense to remove the `34s` from  `DELETECOLLECTION`
- should we allow timeout for DELETECOLLECTION to exceed `60s`?

@deads2k @wojtek-t thoughts?

>The list call that is failing in your case, is a direct call to the storage, right?

It reads from etcd, not from API Server Cache.  Is that what you were asking @tkashem?

Looking at the bigger picture,  I think your question about 60s timeout is a good one. Especially in the context of this: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/90743. In particular, changing the timeouts won't solve all of the problems with DELETECOLLECTION.  My assumption, when logging this issue, is that it might be a quick way to solve just _some_ of them.

> I don't know if it makes sense to remove the 34s from DELETECOLLECTION

I think we should remove this - it's effectively a regression that we introduced with the PR.

> should we allow timeout for DELETECOLLECTION to exceed 60s?

That's a good question, and I'm not entirely sure. Maybe we should, but I would do that separately.

In the meantime, I would much more prefer to switch the DeleteCollection implementation to internally use pagination, as it would allow us to
1) not block on full list (and as a result make some progress)
2) would be some preparation towards potentially exposing a Limit option in the API...


/kind regression
/sig api-machinery
/triage accepted

I suggest the following:

1. @tkashem - can you please take care of reverting the 34s timeout for DeleteCollection calls?
2. Once this is done, let's close this issue and continue operating on https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/90743

@wojtek-t sounds good, thanks!

/assign

title: kubeadm should not pull images for skipped addon phases (coredns, kube-proxy)
body:
### What happened?

- Cluster created with custom CoreDNS installation, i.e. `skipPhases: [ addon/coredns ]` specified in kubeadm init configuration
- When joining a new node using `kubeadm join`, kubeadm still tries to pull all images
- If that image pull fails, kubeadm bails out despite the image not being required. See https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/114978 for how the CoreDNS image pull is special and could therefore fail.

### What did you expect to happen?

No image pull attempt for images belonging to skipped phases.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Not needed. The current functionality is very clear – see `GetControlPlaneImages` in code:

```
// GetControlPlaneImages returns a list of container images kubeadm expects to use on a control plane node
func GetControlPlaneImages(cfg *kubeadmapi.ClusterConfiguration) []string {
	images := make([]string, 0)

	// start with core kubernetes images
	images = append(images, GetKubernetesImage(constants.KubeAPIServer, cfg))
	images = append(images, GetKubernetesImage(constants.KubeControllerManager, cfg))
	images = append(images, GetKubernetesImage(constants.KubeScheduler, cfg))
	images = append(images, GetKubernetesImage(constants.KubeProxy, cfg))

	// pause is not available on the ci image repository so use the default image repository.
	images = append(images, GetPauseImage(cfg))

	// if etcd is not external then add the image as it will be required
	if cfg.Etcd.Local != nil {
		images = append(images, GetEtcdImage(cfg))
	}

	// Append the appropriate DNS images
	images = append(images, GetDNSImage(cfg))

	return images
}
```

### Anything else we need to know?

This also reduces unnecessary network throughput and is therefore in line with [KEP 3000](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-release/3000-artifact-distribution) goals.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubeadm/issues/1842 is quite similar.

title: kubeproxy.config.k8s.io/v1alpha1 Breaking Change
body:
### What happened?

There appears to be a breaking change to kubeproxy.config.k8s.io/v1alpha1 in PR https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/112133

The schema for kubeproxy.config.k8s.io/v1alpha1 changed by removing the `udpIdleTimeout` without being deprecated. 

We based our manifest on what `kubeadm config print init-defaults --component-configs=KubeProxyConfiguration` provided to us in a previous version of kubeadm (pre 1.26)

When we tried create a new cluster with Kubernetes 1.26 using existing configuration we receive this error from kubeadm:

```

This is the equivalent of not being given the name of your accuser in a court of law. :smile: 

Very frustrating for users in multi-tenant environments who are forced to work with the cluster administrators to identify why their pods were preempted.

It might be ok for your multitenant use case not to expose this information, but you cannot speak for every user of kubernetes.

> Very frustrating for users in multi-tenant environments who are forced to work with the cluster administrators to identify why their pods were preempted.

Can you actually give more context? Why do users need to know the name of the preemptor? What would it change? The preemption would still happen. If there are some priorities that need to be adjusted, it shouldn't be on the users to set an arbitrary priority without consulting the administrators.

/sig auth

As the SIG that suggested we hide this information from end-users.

Our monitoring stack (Datadog) indexes all k8s events and makes it very easy for users to identify the source of preemption and reach out to the team that owns the pods when that information is retained in the event message.

This is efficient because the involved teams (preemptor and preemptee) can resolve the issue on their own without involving cluster-admins who are very busy with other work. The mitigations are all user operations, not requiring cluster admin intervention.
1. Address the health of the preempting pods.
2. Adjust the rollout configuration of the preempting pods.
3. Adjust the priority classes to avoid the preemption.

I can also understand supporting cases where a company is offering a multi-tenant environment and tenant A should not see any information, including namespaces and pod names of tenant B. But I would also call out that it's very weird for a Preemption configuration to be in place between two extremely isolated use cases.

Is it unreasonable to support a configuration parameter to allowing higher verbosity in these event messages? We currently allow all multi-tenant users full read access on the k8s scheduler logs, but event data is more readily available to our users.

This was initially proposed by @liggitt , but he's out on vacation.
@deads2k maybe you have some thoughts about this?
One thing I thought weird here is we can preempt the pod but we can't know its name. 🤔

+1 for knowing who caused the pre-emption, it makes debugging bad deploys so much harder if we don't know

Also the [code](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blame/f0dcf0614036d8c3cd1c9f3b3cf8df4bb1d8e44e/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/events/event_recorder.go#L88) seems to still have "Related" field set, but in the actual event that's gone, not sure what's up with that.

---
involvedObject:

  namespace: kube-system
kind: Event
message: Preempted by a pod on node ip-172-30-123-123.us-west-2.compute.internal

  namespace: kube-system
reason: Preempted

reportingInstance: ""
source:
  component: default-scheduler
type: Normal
```

uid sounds like a great compromise

#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

<!--

/kind documentation
/kind feature

Optionally add one or more of the following kinds if applicable:
/kind api-change
/kind deprecation
/kind failing-test
/kind flake
/kind regression
-->

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

This came up when updating go-oidc. After updating go-oidc (with its dependency tree), cloud.google.com/go was no longer used as a package import, but still listed in the module dependency graph; as a result, "go mod vendor" no longer pulled in cloud.google.com/go itself, but update-vendor-licenses.sh still wanted a license file for it since it appeared in the list of modules.

This scenario is already supposed to be handled: when a module doesn't contain any *files* as first-level content, if the number of subdirectories it contains *equals* the number of submodules it contains (excluding itself), the module is skipped. This fails for cloud.google.com/go because several submodules are included in the module dependency graph but aren't actually used, and therefore not vendored.

Updating the test to check that the number of subdirectories is less than or equal to the number of expected submodules fixes this.

The correct fix would be to process the submodules first, keeping a note of which ones really have content, then check that the top-level module only contains subdirectories corresponding to those modules; but it's not clear to me that this is worth the effort (especially in a shell script).

kube-proxy should be generates correct iptables rule

body:
### What happened?

We had a nodePort service which use port 30002, transport to a host-network pod which listen 8002.Now it is invalid , we can't access `nodeIp:30002` , but `nodeIp:8002` is valid.

> why we use nodePort when we already use host-network?
Because it could has multiple replicas, we use nodePort to ensure it's avaliable when one pod is down.

1. we check ipvs rules,it's like :
```
ipvsadm -L -n 
IP Virtual Server version 1.2.1 (size=4096)
Prot LocalAddress:Port Scheduler Flags
  -> RemoteAddress:Port           Forward Weight ActiveConn InActConn
TCP  172.17.0.1:30002 rr
TCP  172.17.0.1:30009 rr
  -> 10.16.203.62:8002
```

We all see , `30002` doesn't have any target.

2. we check endpont status ,it's like:

![1670324387](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/10915774/207255935-e73d8930-fb85-4e14-82b6-cf28ff45191e.png)

We all see , the same ipaddr is both in Addresses and NotReadyAddress.

And , there are some invalid pods and one valid pod , this is why the endpoint looks like.



### What did you expect to happen?

if an ipaddr is both in readyAddrs and notReadyAddrs, it shouled be removed  from notReadyAddrs to make sure that
valid IP addresses are not masked by invalid IP addresses。Then the url `http://nodeIP:30002` we called will always be accessible  whenever the deployment has invalid pods or not.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. apply a pod which use host-network , and bind to a fixed node; the pod shouled not has request and limit value ,ensure is is `BestEffort` , so it will be evicited first.
2. apply a service which use nodePort 30002, and bind to the pod
3. manual  make a Diskpressure which is easily caused by dd a big file.
4. the pod will be evicited ,
5. move the Diskpressure ,And the pod will be created 
6. Then you will reproduce it , the endpoint will has the nodeIp both in readyAddrs and notReadyAddrs.

title: kube-apiserver using unregistered and unusual label
body:
### What happened?

The code at
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/86f3fa94f1b75da275a8040e4155840a7b473dc1/pkg/controlplane/instance.go#L126 specifies a ~annotation~ label that API servers set on Leases (each API server registers its own lease).

https://k8s.io/docs/concepts/architecture/leases/#api-server-identity is likely to document this once v1.26 is released; the alpha for API server identity didn't get documented.

Here's the problems:
- as a project, we use `kubernetes.io` as the domain for labels and annotations - see https://k8s.io/docs/reference/labels-annotations-taints/
  - there are a couple of exceptions in https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/labels-annotations-taints/audit-annotations/, FWIW
- if we document and register this `k8s.io/component` label, people may well confuse it with https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/labels-annotations-taints/#app-kubernetes-io-component and use the wrong thing

### What did you expect to happen?

I guess ideally we'd have proposed and then been able to review docs for this when it went alpha, and in that alternative history the discrepancy would have been much more obvious, and it could have been fixed earlier.

I think we should fix it so that we follow the convention of nearly every other annotation used in Kubernetes code.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

In the worse case when a cluster upgrades from v1.26.0 -> v1.26.1, there will be N (1-5) leases that will never be garbage collected because old leases have labels that the new gc controller is not selecting against. 
2) v1.26 is the first version where this is enabled by default, so we shouldn't anticipate many existing consumers of the lease or use of that label. In the worse case we end up with a handful of leases that aren't garbage collected like in 1).
3) No one is _really_ going to use v1.26.0 :)

If we _really_ care about the v1.26.0 -> v1.26.1 corner case, we can update GC controller to garbage collect leases with both labels `k8s.io/component=kube-apiserver` and `internal.kubernetes.io/component`

When other (usually external) projects or components aren't using labels or annotations the recommended way, I usually recommend handling the old deprecated key for a while (or even indefinitely), but mentioning the fixed key in documentation.

So, that sounds good. I don't feel that a fix is urgent, but I do recommend against leaving it this way all the way to v1.27.0

Summarizing discussion we had on this in SIG API Machinery today:
* We're going to move the identity lease controller and GC controller to generic apiserver (as part of https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/114240), with optional flags to set the lease namespace and component label value. These will always be configured in kube-apiserver in the `kube-system` namespace, but off by default for any aggregated apiservers pulling in generic apiserver.
* The label key / value for `kube-apiserver` will change to something that follows documented best practices, which _should_ be safe as long as GC controller is updated to watch both the old and new labels until v1.28.
* There should be a Role defined to manged identities that any aggregated apiserver can bind to for their own system namespaces

title: windows cpu maximum incorrect with more than one processor group
body:
### What happened?

When submitting a windows pod using resource limits on a node with more than one processor group, the specified `CpuMaximum` count is incorrect due to the usage of `runtime.NumCPU()` which does not take processor groups into account.

For example:
- node with 96 cores
- cpu limit 94
- `runtime.NumCPU()` returns `48`

This results in a CPU maximum of 10000 since the range is from [1, 10000]:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_container_windows.go#L82..L91

```go
	limit := int64(94 * 1000)
	numCPU := 48
	fmt.Println(((10000 * limit) / int64(numCPU) / 1000))

// Output:
// 19583
```

Our initial goal for this was to limit a process to not use all available CPU and therefore render the node uncontrollable. 

### What did you expect to happen?

A CPU maximum of `9791` instead of `10000` for that specific case. For the calculation, it should use the CPU count for all available processor groups instead of just the current one. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Launch a node with a lot of CPUs, for example [a Azure Standard_D96a_v4](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/dav4-dasv4-series) and schedule the following pod on it:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: debug-windows
  namespace: default
spec:
  containers:
  - args:
    - ping /t 127.0.0.1
    command:
    - cmd
    - /c
    image: mcr.microsoft.com/windows/nanoserver:1809
    imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
    name: main
    resources:
      limits:
        cpu: "94"
        memory: 300Gi
      requests:
        cpu: "90"
        memory: 200Gi
  nodeSelector:
    kubernetes.io/os: windows
```

Then SSH into the node and inspect the running container using `crictl.exe inspect <id>`. The `cpu_maximum` value will be set to 10000. 

### Anything else we need to know?

[tklauser/numcpus](https://github.com/tklauser/numcpus) (which just uses [`windows.GetActiveProcessorCount()`](https://pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/sys/windows#GetActiveProcessorCount)) is able to correctly find out the number of CPUs available to a system. Using `golang.org/x/sys/windows` for calculation or incorporating that code might solve this issue.

title: Ephemeral container fails to be created for Static Pod
body:
### What happened?

I created an ephemeral container for a Static Pod using the `kubectl debug` command. The command succeed.

```console
❯ kubectl debug --image=busybox --share-processes=true --target=kube-apiserver -n kube-system kube-apiserver-kind-control-plane -- sleep infinity
Targeting container "kube-apiserver". If you don't see processes from this container it may be because the container runtime doesn't support this feature.
Defaulting debug container name to debugger-vgkn4.
```



The API server accepted the ephemeral container:
```console
❯ kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-apiserver-kind-control-plane --output=jsonpath='{.spec.ephemeralContainers}'
[{"command":["sleep","infinity"],"image":"busybox","imagePullPolicy":"Always","name":"debugger-vgkn4","resources":{},"targetContainerName":"kube-apiserver","terminationMessagePath":"/dev/termination-log","terminationMessagePolicy":"File"}]
```

However, the container is not created.

Its status is also not available:

```console
❯ kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-apiserver-kind-control-plane --output=jsonpath='{.status.ephemeralContainerStatuses}'

```

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected one of these:

(a) the API server rejects the request to create an ephemeral container for a Static Pod
(b) kubelet creates the ephemeral container, and update the Static Pod's status sub-resource

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Using a recent version of [docker engine](https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/), [kind](https://kind.sigs.k8s.io/docs/user/quick-start/)  v0.17 or newer, and [kubectl](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/tools/#kubectl) v1.25.0 or newer, create a cluster and create an ephemeral container running `sleep infinity`. docker exec -it kind-control-plane ps -axw | grep --count "sleep infinity"
```


### Anything else we need to know?

The [Ephemeral Containers KEP](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-node/277-ephemeral-containers/README.md) does not address Static Pods.

title: Kubectl restmapping cache causes inconsistent behaviour in case of resource name conflict
body:
### What happened?

I deployed a CRD (`teleportroles`) with the shortnames `role` and `roles`, conflicting with `roles.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1`.

Initially `kubectl get role` and `kubectl get roles` were both returnning `roles.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1` resources.

I ran `kubectl get teleportrole`.

Now, `kubectl get role` return my CRs instead of `roles.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1` resources.

However `kubectl get roles` continues to return `roles.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1` resources.

### What did you expect to happen?

I expect kubectl's behaviour to be consistent. The outcome of `kubectl get X` should not depend on the order the APIs were discovered and cached. I also expect exact names to be preferred over shortnames.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

On a freshly kubectl context (not one you already used and might have cached RESTMappings):
- create a CRD with a shortname conflicting with another resource, `role` for example
- run `kubectl get role -n kube-sytem` (because there are roles by default there) and `kubectl get roles -n kube-system`
- observe the kube rbac resources are properly returned
- run `kubectl get yourcrd` once
- run `kubectl get role -n kube-sytem` (because there are roles by default there) and `kubectl get roles -n kube-system`
- observe the `kubectl get role` no longer returns the kubernetes roles, but `kubectl get roles` still does. 

### Anything else we need to know?

During initial resolution, [exact name matches are preferred](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/58861). It seems this property is not true anymore when doing cache lookups. When cache was populated by `kubectl get teleportroles`, it overrode the mapping `role` -> `roles.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1`

I believe this is the same issue as https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/59812

$ kubectl version

nodes.body: /sig cli
This looks like a duplicate of these https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/102378, https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/108573

If I understand correctly those two issues are feature requests to warn users in case of conflict, I would not consider them duplicates of this one.

Here, the issue is not the conflict, but kubectl not consistently choosing the same resource (and also not prioritizing extact name matches over shortnames as it should). The returned  resources depend on the last cached RESTmapping, which depends on the order the commands are run.

The following snippets currently have very different behaviours:
```bash
kubectl get role
kubectl get teleportrole
kubectl delete role my-role  # deletes a teleportrole
```

```bash
kubectl get role
kubectl delete role my-role  # deletes a rbac role
```

This can be harmful in CI environments when each job has a fresh RESTMapping cache.

Note: I'm talking about kubectl but the issue lives in go-client caching mechanism. I guess this not only affects filesystem cache but also memory cache, which means operators or other tools leveraging go-client could also face the same inconsistencies when discovering apis.
I'm going to investigate this issue.

I've sorted out the problem and this is a nice finding and can be easily reproduced by running this [unit test](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f7d1eb7726fa511b6439b7f8162138742ac639ab/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/restmapper/shortcut_test.go#L121) with empty `SingularName`.

when user runs;
```sh
kubectl get role
```
The expectation is that shortcut expands singular form `role` to `roles` after matching `singularName` in [this line](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f7d1eb7726fa511b6439b7f8162138742ac639ab/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/restmapper/shortcut.go#L142). However, this does not happen because for core types discovery endpoint does not return `singularName` field other than empty. As a result, this conditional is never true for core types.

`kubectl get role` returns `roles` up to now as expected because after shortcut could not expand this to any kind(also not in CRD shortcuts), it asks defaultRESTMapper in best effort. `role` is already expanded in this [unsafe function](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f229ef70764fcb4bda69c8a7af645bab67f4ecca/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/api/meta/restmapper.go#L100)

But as in this case, if there is a CRD matching as shortcut, shortcut returns that and this creates nondeterministic behavior.

Workaround solution would be;

If `singularName` is not match, we can also search `role` in all apiresource list in singular form(by using `UnsafeGuessKindToResource`). But we may not want this due to statement in [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f229ef70764fcb4bda69c8a7af645bab67f4ecca/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/api/meta/restmapper.go#L123-L125)

Permanent solution would be;

We can introduce `SingularNameProvider`(like being done for [shortNames](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/40985)) and use it in [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/57c95fbfa12bc04456330d8b0b29f333106cf156/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/endpoints/installer.go#L991) to let discovery can also return singular names of core types. 

@liggitt would you mind if I ask your opinions about the solutions?

/triage accepted

nodes.title: Set singular names for core types to pass to discovery
nodes.body:
#### What type of PR is this?
/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
Core types don't set their singular names for discovery endpoint(as opposed to CRDs).
This results in nondeterministic behavior when there is a CRD whose shortname is
one of core types singular name format. Thereby, when user requests resource via this short name,
it becomes unpredictable(because it is determined by the order of which one is requested first).

This PR adds singular names for all core types. As a result, core types will
have always higher precedence when their singular name format is requested
regardless of request order.

#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:
Fixes #113227

#### Special notes for your reviewer:
In terms of backwards compatibility, this change has negative impact only on the use cases where people currently are expecting CRDs via singular form of core types. Isn't this already extreme case and incorrect expectation?
#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?
```release-note
None
```

For a service of type Loadbalancer, the BIRD speaker on a node advertises the Loadbalancer IP to DCGW on a BGP session when a service pod comes up on the same node. When the service pod(serving TCP traffic)) is deleted, the pod comes up on a different node and speaker on this node now advertises the LB IP to the DCGW.  The TCP traffic which was earlier destined to the deleted pod, is now routed to the new pod on this node. This traffic includes:
1. **New TCP SYN connection requests**. After 15s client side disconnect connections that were in status SYN_SENT since connection was not able to be established. Corresponding conntrack entries are removed after about 2 minutes. So this is not an issue.
2. **Existing TCP connections in ESTABLISHED state**. These are now the midstream packets for this endpoint. Sometimes, it is observed that the speaker advertisement is faster than the kube-proxy setting up the IPTABLE rules to the new endpoint. Since no rule has been setup yet this defaults to dropping the packet. When the first packet arrives, a conntrack entry is registered and updates the entry as UNREPLIED. All the subsequent incoming packets with the same tuple that arrive updates the conntrack entry with updated expiry timer. Unless this conntrack entry is deleted or client terminates the connection, the subsequent packets can not be handled as the timer would never expire. A possible solution would be to delete stale conntrack entries before setting up the IPTABLE rules for the given service.

title: Kubelet overrides (non-empty) container metrics from CRI with empty cAdvisor metrics
body:
### What happened?

Container / Pod Stats reported by kubelet are currently collected by cAdvisor (and optionally CRI).  As seen in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/107172, currently cAdvisor metrics override CRI metrics. This is an issue for some runtimes such as gVisor container which do not export cgroupfs metrics but export CRI metrics. 

As a result, currently for cases when CRI metrics are reported as non-empty and cAdvisor metrics are empty (gVisor is such an example), kubelet overrides the metrics with the empty cAdvisor ones and thus does not report metrics. 




### What did you expect to happen?

Kubelet should not override CRI metrics with cAdvisor ones if the CRI metrics are non-empty and the cAdvisor ones are empty. 


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Run a gVisor container and check if metrics are being reported (e.g. via the /metrics/resource endpoint).

### Anything else we need to know?

This issue has been fixed in 1.25 with #110950 since #110950 filters out empty cAdvisor metrics and thus will use CRI metrics if cAdvisor metrics are missing. Suggest to cherrypick #110950 to older versions.

### Kubernetes version

1.24 and below (found as issue on 1.22-1.24). Fixed on 1.25.

title: CSI SetUpAt does not retry when STAGE_UNSTAGE_VOLUME check fails
body:
### What happened?

We've noticed occasionally the following scenario:

1. Deployment with CSI volumes is created
2. CSI driver goes down immediately before/after deployment is created
3. Kubelet fails to check for `STAGE_UNSTAGE_VOLUME` capability https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/64ed9145452d2d1d324d2437566f1ea1ce76f226/pkg/volume/csi/csi_mounter.go#L172-L174
4. If the CSI driver takes a minute or so to start back up, the `SetUpAt` calls are not retried.

My guess is that `NodeSupportsStageUnstage` is returning a "final" error that results in no more retries from the kubelet.

When the kubelet was restarted,
1. the kubelet immediately retried the calls
2. our CSI Driver mounted the volumes
3. the remaining two pods went to `Running` state. 

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected retries to occur forever until a CSI driver is healthy again

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create a deployment referencing CSI volumes when the CSI driver has just become unhealthy.

```

```

title: Regression: Move canSafelySkipMountPointCheck out of mount-utils Interface
body:
### What happened?

`CanSafelySkipMountPointCheck` was made "package private" (i.e. renamed to `canSafelySkipMountPointCheck `) in https://github.com/kubernetes/mount-utils/commit/a20fcfb15a701977d086330b47b7efad51eb608 (which pulls from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/983a570b9e3e48259c91d7264bbfbcfd91eb6d66).

We mock `mount-utils.Interface` in the AWS EBS CSI Driver for testing but `mockgen`'s implementation no longer is valid because it cannot implement the `canSafelySkipMountPointCheck`.

### What did you expect to happen?

Ability to implement `mount-utils.Interface` *outside* of the `mount-utils` package.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

N/A

### Anything else we need to know?

I considered reporting this on the mount-utils repo itself but its issue tracker seems to be unused/abandoned. Let me know if there's a more appropriate place to report.

If it is intended for `canSafelySkipMountPointCheck` to be private this can easily be fixed by moving it out of the `mount-utils.Interface` interface.

title: kubelet event about unattached volumes is incorrect
body:
### What happened?

1. Create Pod with unattachable volume A and B and make A unable to mount
2. The Pod will be in `ContainerCreating` state
3. Wait for several minutes, then show the pod events by `kubectl describe pod`
4. The events information includes error msg like
    ```shell
     Warning  FailedMount  3m48s (x2 over 6m2s)  kubelet            Unable to attach or mount volumes: unmounted volumes=[A], unattached volumes=[A, B]: timed out waiting for the condition
    ```
5. The error msg is confusing since it indicates that A and B are unattached

### What did you expect to happen?

The events show correct information about unmounted volumes and unattached volumes.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Use following yaml and do the test as posted above:

```yaml
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: myapp
  labels:
    name: myapp
spec:
  containers:
  - name: myapp
    image: nginx
    resources:
      limits:
        memory: "128Mi"
        cpu: "500m"
    volumeMounts:
      - name: test-cm1
        mountPath: /test-cm1
      - name: test-cm2
        mountPath: /test-cm2
      - name: test-ebs
        mountPath: /test-ebs
  volumes:
    - name: test-cm1  # unattachable, succeed to mount
      configMap:
        name: test-cm1
    - name: test-cm2  # unattachable, fail to mount
      configMap:
        name: noexist
    - name: test-ebs   # attachable, fail to attach and mount
      awsElasticBlockStore:
        volumeID: "test"
        fsType: ext4
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: test-cm1
data:
  key: value
```

title: scheduler: The scoring logic of ImageLocality does not seem to take effect
body:
### What happened?

The ImageLocality policy is used to schedule pods. The actual scheduling result shows that the policy does not take effect. Open the scheduler log to view details (--v=11). The scheduler (ImageLocality policy) scores all nodes that have images required for creating pods with zero scores.

1. Configure the kube-scheduler scheduling policy.
    ```
    apiVersion: kubescheduler.config.k8s.io/v1beta2
    kind: KubeSchedulerConfiguration
    clientConnection:
      kubeconfig: /etc/kubernetes/scheduler.conf
    profiles:
      - schedulerName: default-scheduler
      - schedulerName: wy-scheduler
        plugins:
          score:
            enabled:
              - name: ImageLocality 
                weight: 100
              - name: TaintToleration
                weight: 0
              - name: NodeAffinity
                weight: 0
              - name: PodTopologySpread
                weight: 0
              - name: NodeResourcesBalancedAllocation
                weight: 0
              - name: InterPodAffinity
                weight: 0
    ```
2. The K8S cluster has three work nodes. Load only the `nginx:job-test` image required for creating pods in `k8s-1.23-worker`.

/sig scheduling

The cause of the problem has been found. During image name matching, one function has not been implemented, as shown in the following figure.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ed8c302cc602023e07be4dabe89a87184f718d56/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/imagelocality/image_locality.go#L116-L126

The name of the image loaded to the host is `docker.io/library/nginx:job-test`. The name of the image in the YAML file is `nginx:job-test`. The names are different. As a result, the matching fails. The value of the imagelocality policy is 0.

Change the value of image in the YAML file from `nginx:job-test` to `docker.io/library/nginx:job-test`.
In terms of user usage, this should be a bug. Do we have a fix plan in the future?

/cc
I'll take a look later today.

~We have two approaches:~
~1) One is happened in writing. When `addNodeImageStates`, we'll add a familiarizeName see https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/c86e3d85d9507b7abe774d7852c7de9cd51d4819.
Then we have to modify several places to keep the logic in consistent, like `addNodeImageStates`, `removeNodeImageStates` and so on. It will add the maintenance cost.~

~2) Another approach is happened in reading. When finding matched image name, we'll add the `docker.io/library` header if needed. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ef56451ae52407af16647214865e4818eb2ac958/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/imagelocality/image_locality.go#L97-L105~

cc @kubernetes/sig-scheduling-leads for thoughts. 

Rephrased: 
we may have to set the image name to a familiar name both in reading and writing. For example, "docker.io/library/redis" will have the familiar name "redis" and "docker.io/dmcgowan/myapp" will be "dmcgowan/myapp".

I don't think we can assume that the image runtime is docker and that the default registry is docker.io

If anything, I believe this should be fixed in kubelet or CRI when filling up `node.Status.Images`

But we can avoid this to some extent by getting the familiarizeName. For example, "docker.io/library/redis" will have the familiar name "redis" and "docker.io/dmcgowan/myapp" will be "dmcgowan/myapp".  Then both in reading and writing from the cache, we'll tune the image name to the familiar name in calculating.
But what if they are not using docker to pull the images? @SergeyKanzhelev any insight on what can be done to match image names?

> In terms of user usage, this should be a bug. Do we have a fix plan in the future?

This isn't a bug on the scheduler side. The scheduler doesn't know, and probably shouldn't, how the on-node processes handle image names. Indeed, the only option here is for kubelet to update node status with all applicable names for the image.
Doesn't this only happened on docker runtime? Making the image names explicit is better I think, this is consistent with other runtimes.

title: Change in semantics for the device plugin registration process
body:
### What happened?

The following refactoring of the kubelet's devicemanager was done as part of the 1.25 release: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/db88676c20629354d8eeb4b7014ae7884481ffca

As part of this, a change in semantics was (unintentionally) introduced which is breaking at least one 3rd party plugin. The logic required to go back to the old semantics is fairly straight forward. However, it's not obvious that we should actually go back to the old semantics because (at least in my opinion) the new semantics are actually more correct.

Previously, the kubelet's devicemanager would do the following upon receiving a plugin registration request:
1. Register the plugin
2. Launch a go-routine to connect to the gRPC service being served by the plugin (with a timeout of 10s)
3. Return

This gave the plugin the opportunity to first register itself with the kubelet and then (within a 10s time window) start its gRPC server.

The new semantics are similar, except that no go-routine is launched to connect to the gRPC service. The connection is attempted synchronously. This means that the plugin must now start serving its gRPC server *before* registering itself with the kubelet. Otherwise the registration call will fail.

As mentioned before, this change was not necessarily intentional, but it's also not clear if it should be reverted. It brings the device plugin's custom registration process more in line with the kubelet's standard registration process and the order is actually a bit more intuitive. Why bother registering if you aren't able to start serving your API?

The first plugin to report this problem was the KubeVirt plugin and a discussion of the issue can be found here:
https://groups.google.com/g/kubevirt-dev/c/HE2lVvsLd3Y

The question now is -- should we revert the kubelet code to the old semantics to avoid breaking plugins that rely on this (somewhat awkward) ordering. Or do we leave the new semantics in place and send out an announcement of this (potentially) breaking change?

One thing to keep in mind -- if we go with the second option (i.e. keep the new semantics and force plugins to update), the updated plugins will continue to work on older versions of kubernetes since the ordering now implied in the new semantics has always been correct.

### What did you expect to happen?

Plugins relying on the old semantics would continue to work on kubernetes 1.25

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Write a plugin that:
1. Registers itself with the kubelet
2. Only then starts to server the plugin API via a gRPC server

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

/cc @fromanirh 
/cc @derekwaynecarr 
/cc @RenaudWasTaken
/sig node
xref: https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/pull/8451

I'm interested in the fact that the e2e tests didn't seem to catch this issue. Besides improving our coverage, which rarely hurts, I tend to believe that one of the key factors is that we use sample-device-plugin in the e2e tests, which is understandably updated in lockstep with the core k/k code. I wonder how we can improve in this area, perhaps using _also_ a known set of 3rd party device plugins as part as e2e testing?

The plugin used in the e2e tests uses the standard kubelet plugin registration method (i.e. the one that relies on the plugin dropping a socket file in a well known location to trigger the registration), not the custom / legacy one used by the KubeVirt (and potentially many other) plugins.

TL;DR: if the broken plugins were doing legitimate things (-> were not themselves buggy) we should fix the kube side, even if the new process really seems better.

My initial though is this is the right change done the wrong way. The new registration process should be enabled - for all the good reason @klueska listed - but we should have better docs and a transition process (e.g. deprecating the old process, supporting both for a little while... details to be figured out).

Now: the device manager is stil a [beta feature in 1.25](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.25.0/pkg/features/kube_features.go#L247) (!!!!!!) so we have some slack space, but still this change breaks some device plugins which, AFAIK, were not buggy in the area of the registration process (is my understanding right?). This is not ok for a beta feature AFAIK, and not great in general.

I reserve myself to review in deeper detail and come back, but IMO we should treat this like a bug and revert the change, *then* work towards the better registration process.
/cc @bart0sh

/triage accepted
/assign @fromanirh 
/priority important-soon

> but still this change breaks some device plugins which, AFAIK, were not buggy in the area of the registration process (is my understanding right?)

FWIW, the sequence is [documented](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/extend-kubernetes/compute-storage-net/device-plugins/#device-plugin-implementation) and it says the plugin starts a gRPC service and then registers itself.

Agree with @fromanirh at least we should give time and proper notification to device plugin owners, so:
1. revert it for now
2. add a deprecation message under device manager, that will inform plugins owners to update their device plugins(and probably we also should have updated documentation that will explain the correct way to initialize now the device plugin)
3. revert the revert after one or two releases :)
1.-3. sounds overkill if it's just one plugin that was not following the doc and needs fixing.

> As part of this, a change in semantics was (unintentionally) introduced which is breaking at least one 3rd party plugin. The logic required to go back to the old semantics is fairly straight forward. However, it's not obvious that we should actually go back to the old semantics because (at least in my opinion) the new semantics are actually more correct.

I tend to agree that the new semantics (starting gRPC server before registration) are more intuitive and correct.
> The question now is -- should we revert the kubelet code to the old semantics to avoid breaking plugins that rely on this (somewhat awkward) ordering. Or do we leave the new semantics in place and send out an announcement of this (potentially) breaking change?

Based the following points, I am inclining towards the latter (sticking to the new semantics and updating device plugins impacted by this change):

- the documentation already captures the correct ordering
- the plugin that brought this issue to light has already been [updated](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/pull/8451)
- a plugin once updated would continue to work on older versions of Kubernetes

Reverting the change seems like a step back when we can handle this by sending out communication to highlight the potential issue and capturing explicitly in the documentation that "a device plugin **must** start serving gRPC server before registering itself".
I created a small docs [PR](https://github.com/kubernetes/website/pull/36940) to update the documentation (which can be used if there is consensus to proceed in this direction).

So @mythi and @swatisehgal pointed out that the correct ordering was already documented. Then the basic assumption in my previous https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/112395#issuecomment-1246475947 is void. I'll have a deeper review myself ASAP, but if this is the case, then retroactively fixing the docs and sending a late announcement seems indeed the best approach, and reverting the changes turns from "overkill" to "actually wrong". I'll update ASAP.

> So @mythi and @swatisehgal pointed out that the correct ordering was already documented. Then the basic assumption in my previous [#112395 (comment)](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/112395#issuecomment-1246475947) is void. I'll have a deeper review myself ASAP, but if this is the case, then retroactively fixing the docs and sending a late announcement seems indeed the best approach, and reverting the changes turns from "overkill" to "actually wrong". I'll update ASAP.

So the[ device plugin flow](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/extend-kubernetes/compute-storage-net/device-plugins/#device-plugin-implementation) was documented in its current form (which is not broken by the change we're discussing) [since 2018](https://github.com/kubernetes/website/commit/169aadbbe185b6c42c8f2a4e8066548903b72d12)

Then yes, my initial reaction is overtuned. It would probably have be nice to give the device plugin author some leniency before to enforce the correct flow as we did by accident, but the fact the kube code enforces the documented, expected flow still stands. So we better handle this issue with a documentation update and/or a release note update.

title: client-go's InClusterConfig does not implement documented API discovery heuristics
body:
### What happened?

client-go uses `KUBERNETES_SERVICE_HOST` to discover the API service address:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/67bde9a1023d1805e33d698b28aa6fad991dfb39/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/rest/config.go#L507-L541 

This at odds with the documentation at https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/run-application/access-api-from-pod/#directly-accessing-the-rest-api which states:

> While running in a Pod, the Kubernetes apiserver is accessible via a Service named `kubernetes` in the `default` namespace. Therefore, Pods can use the `kubernetes.default.svc` hostname to query the API server. Official client libraries do this automatically.

client-go does **not** do this. Though, it includes a TODO:

```go
		// TODO: switch to using cluster DNS.
		Host:            "https://" + net.JoinHostPort(host, port),
```

Ambiguity around the documented client discovery policy causes problems for client libraries; and cloud providers continue to promulgate the (now undocumented) legacy env configuration, e.g. https://github.com/Azure/AKS/issues/3183.

Would you accept a PR to remove the environment based in-cluster configuration in favor of always using `kubernetes.default.svc`?

### What did you expect to happen?

client-go should use `kubernetes.default.svc` and it should not honor the `KUBERNETES_SERVICE_HOST` environment variable.

OR the client docs should be updated with the proper heuristics.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

nodes.title: Fix in-cluster API discovery documentation
nodes.body:
The documentation incorrectly describes the way that client libraries discover the Kubernetes API server. While the `kubernetes.default.svc` DNS is provided as a convenience, **all** of the officially supported API clients use environment variables to discover the address of the API server.

title: Each time a pod exits, kubelet cpu usage increases with cgroups v2
body:
### What happened?

When a pod exits, there is some problem in the cgroup cleanup. The containerd cgroup within the kubelet cgroup does not get deleted, and then the kubelet keeps trying to delete the kubelet cgroup, which fails because of the child cgroup. The kubelet continues to try to delete the cgroup every 1 second or so. As pods start and stop, the number of cgroups in this state grows, and the kubelet process itself gradually consumes more and more cpu, until it gets to 100% of available.

Here are snippets of the /var/log/syslog for a single example. This is for the case of kubelet cgroup /sys/fs/cgroup/kubepods.slice/kubepods-burstable.slice/kubepods-burstable-podde737447_24b2_4f9e_a805_ad1161a169fb.slice which contains a sub-cgroup cri-containerd-67620447e632a1b3edb19fe05a2b44211cffb996bf6ba5ff52811a8bf32eb8b7.scope.

Hi there, can you please provide repro steps, we are not seeing this issue in any of the cgroupv2 CI jobs, e.g. https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-node-containerd#cos-cgroupv2-containerd-e2e

Another question, is your containerd config set up to use systemd cgroup driver as well?

Additionally, the kubelet version here is quite old (1.22). Does this repro on e.g. 1.24 or 1.25?

This seems that it may be related to other issues being tracked in k8s here https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/112124 as well as OpenShift https://github.com/okd-project/okd/issues/1310
The same messages appear, same CPU usage, as well as some other messages as referenced in these two issues (kubelet_getters.go:300] "Path does not exist" xxxxxxx).

I have 3 clusters on 1.24.0 with the same issue myself, OpenShift 4.11. For me, the control planes run out of memory every 3 days or so. the workers more sporadic. but it seems to relate to the number of pods created, then later deleted, so things such as jobs make it easiest to replicate.

Hmm, have you seen https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/112124#issuecomment-1245903967, it seems related (systemd is overloaded and unable to stop the unit).

Also, is this issue cgroup v2 related? The OS mentioned above (Ubuntu 20.04.5 does not enable cgroupv2 by default; Ubuntu only enables cgroupv2 starting from 22.04+).

Yes, we are running cgroups v2. We enabled it in the kernel. We are running on Amazon EKS. The highest k8s version they support is 1.23, and that was only released 4 weeks ago. That is why we are on 1.22. It is not possible to test this config on 1.24 or 1.25. I think it could be an issue with runc and cgroups v2, but am not sure. I do not see how systemd overload could be the problem. We are not running massive loads. In fact under testing we have a very minimal load on the system as a whole.
@MatthewFagan i would be good to escalate this to the EKS team then?

Hi, one of the above mentioned issues was opened by me. We still have this problem on 4 production clusters. After a few days running a lot of cronjobs kubelet starts consuming multiple 10GBs of RAM and sooner or later gets OOM killed. The problem started to appear after upgrading to v1.24.X on each cluster.

Can you folks provide a bit more details around the setup / possible repro steps? I tried to repro on a 1.24 Ubuntu 20.04 cgroupv2 cluster but was not able to.

* kubelet version
* os version
* Is cgroupv2 enabled or not in the OS image?
* container runtime version (containerd/cri-o) / runc verison
* cgroup driver used
* Repro steps (what the cronjobs are doing (pod specs?), how many are running, etc)

Hi, We found our problem was caused by a high disk io. On the busy work node, the containerd mounted disk io was so high that short-life pods' rootfs couldn't be umounted immediately. Those umount reqs was put to the cri clean queen of the kubelet. The airflow/jenkins got a timeout and recreated more tasks to retry made the situation even worse. 

After changed disk type to faster ssd, all problems has gone. Furthermore, we find our s3 based distribution file system was using a cache policy which is not matched with this cluster's workload. Filesystem's cache dir was sharing same device with containerd. The wrong cache policy used a lot of disk io bandwidth which also slowed down the containerd's clean process. We changed filesystem's cache policy. Now even use a hdd disk type with debian11, the high cpu usage of the kubelet is unable to observe.

I don't know if this is also applicable to other scenarios, FYI

title: Statefuleset/DaemonSet reports invalid status due to ResourceQuota.
body:
### What happened?

When we limited the number of pods for the namespace (let's say 2), then after we deployed the StatefulSet with 5 replicas. Only 2 pods were launched. This is expected behavior but when we see the status of StatefulSet it shows only 1 pod under the `Ready` column. It should show 2 pods in the column.

```
$ kubectl get resourcequota -n test2
NAME       AGE   REQUEST     LIMIT
pj-quota   50m   pods: 2/2   


$ kubectl get pod -n test2
NAME      READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
test2-0   1/1     Running   0          37m
test2-1   1/1     Running   0          36m

$ kubectl get sts -n test2
NAME    READY   AGE
test2   1/5     33m
```

A similar issue also occurred with DaemonSet. When we deployed the DaemonSet in the namespace (on which limited the pod) on the multi-node cluster(1 master node, 2 workers node), it deployed one pod on 2 nodes out of 3 nodes. which is the expected behavior. But the same issue here when we see the status for DaemonSet. It shows 1 pod under the `CURRENT` and `UP-TO-DATE`  column and 0 pods under the `READY` and  `AVAILABLE` column. It should show 2 pods in these columns.

```
$ kubectl get resourcequota -n test
NAME       AGE    REQUEST     LIMIT
pj-quota   141m   pods: 2/2   

$ kubectl get pod -n test
NAME          READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
test2-lj58r   1/1     Running   0          5m19s
test2-xhq2m   1/1     Running   0          5m19s

$ kubectl get daemonset -n test
NAME    DESIRED   CURRENT   READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE   NODE SELECTOR   AGE
test2   3         1         0       1            0           <none>          5m57s
```

It is only when we apply ResourceQuota in the namespace. If we don't apply ResourceQuota then it shows the expected status for the DaemonSet and StatefulSet.

I also checked this behavior with Deployment also, but in that case, it works fine.

```
$ kubectl get deployment -n test3
NAME              READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE   AGE
test-deployment   2/4     2            2           23s
```

### What did you expect to happen?

Statefuleset and DaemonSet should show the correct status when we applied ResourceQuota in the namespace.

For this specific issue it should show like:

**StatefulSet:**
```
$ kubectl get sts -n test2
NAME    READY   AGE
test2   2/5     33m

```
**DaemonSet:**
```
$ kubectl get daemonset -n test
NAME    DESIRED   CURRENT   READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE   NODE SELECTOR   AGE
test2   3         2         2       2            2           <none>          5m57s
```

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1) Set up the multinode cluster (1 master, 2worker nodes):

> minikube start --nodes 3 -p multinode-demo

2) Create 2 namespaces one for StatefulSet and one for DaemonSet:

>$ kubectl create ns test

>$ kubectl create ns test2

3) Apply the below ResourceQuota yaml to both namespaces:
```
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: pj-quota
spec:
  hard:
    pods: "2"
```

4) In namespace `test2` applies below yaml's for StatefulSet:

**svc.yaml:**

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: test2
  labels:
    app: test2
spec:
  ports:
  - port: 80
  clusterIP: None
  selector:
    app: test2
```

**sts.yaml:**

```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  labels:
    app: test2
  name: test2
spec:
  replicas: 5
  serviceName: "test2"
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: test2
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: test2
    spec:
      containers:
      - command:
        - sh
        - -c
        - "while :; do echo hogehoge; sleep 5 & wait; done"

        imagePullPolicy: Always
        name: cli1
```
Now check the following commands:
> kubectl get pod -n test2
> kubectl get sts -n test2

4) In namespace `test` applies below yaml for DeamonSet:

daemonset.yaml:

```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  labels:
    app: test2
  name: test2
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:

title: DeleteCollection API fails if request body is non-empty
body:
### What happened?

In v1.25.0, invoking the DeleteCollection API with a non-empty request body fails with HTTP 500 - the error message is `no kind "DeleteOptions" is registered for version "meta.k8s.io/v1" in scheme "pkg/api/legacyscheme/scheme.go:30"`

All DeleteCollection APIs are specced (in the OpenAPI spec, eg `deleteCoreV1CollectionNamespacedPod` for the repro below) to take a `DeleteOptions` in the request body, and the simplest such value is `{}`. I maintain the Rust API client library, and my library's generated code always sets the request body to `{}` when all the delete options are default (the serialized form of a `DeleteOptions` with no set fields), which is how I noticed this bug.

### What did you expect to happen?

This works with v1.24 and earlier.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

(This repro uses `curl` for full control of the request headers and body.)

1. Create kind cluster of v1.25.0

1. Create client-cert.pem containing the private key and cert extracted from kubectl config. (curl's `--cert` expects PEM-encoded private key followed by PEM-encoded cert in the file.)

    ```sh
    (kubectl config view -o json --raw | jq '.users[0].user["client-certificate-data"]' -r | base64 -d; kubectl config view -o json --raw | jq '.users[0].user["client-key-data"]' -r | base64 -d) >client-cert.pem
    ```

1. Try to delete all pods with label `foo=bar`

    ```sh
    $ base="$(kubectl config view -o json --raw | jq '.clusters[0].cluster.server' -r)"

    $ curl -kD - -XDELETE --cert client-cert.pem -H 'content-type:application/json' -H 'content-length:2' --data-raw '{}' "${base}/api/v1/namespaces/default/pods?labelSelector=foo%3Dbar"

    HTTP/2 500 
    audit-id: b3c6ed2c-1e53-48a7-8a7c-324706c86ae3
    cache-control: no-cache, private
    content-type: application/json
    x-kubernetes-pf-flowschema-uid: 9fb6dbeb-e6fc-4635-aa6a-7f719dfb1580
    x-kubernetes-pf-prioritylevel-uid: cf4b1a36-f72a-4231-acd7-8e133364d160
    content-length: 235
    date: Wed, 24 Aug 2022 03:11:33 GMT

    {
      "kind": "Status",
      "apiVersion": "v1",
      "metadata": {},
      "status": "Failure",
      "message": "no kind \"DeleteOptions\" is registered for version \"meta.k8s.io/v1\" in scheme \"pkg/api/legacyscheme/scheme.go:30\"",
      "code": 500
    }
    ```

    The same request without a request body succeeds:

    ```sh
    $ curl -kD - -XDELETE --cert client-cert.pem -H 'content-type:application/json' "${base}/api/v1/namespaces/default/pods?labelSelector=foo%3Dbar"

    HTTP/2 200 
    audit-id: 896f90da-7aa1-415d-9c0e-e94b4bd3bea1
    cache-control: no-cache, private
    content-type: application/json
    x-kubernetes-pf-flowschema-uid: 9fb6dbeb-e6fc-4635-aa6a-7f719dfb1580
    x-kubernetes-pf-prioritylevel-uid: cf4b1a36-f72a-4231-acd7-8e133364d160
    content-length: 111
    date: Wed, 24 Aug 2022 03:12:53 GMT

    {
      "kind": "PodList",
      "apiVersion": "v1",
      "metadata": {
        "resourceVersion": "5203"
      },
      "items": []
    }
    ```

nodes.body: /sig api-machinery

/cc @Jefftree 
/triage accepted

This is pretty bad because it's not even a backwards-compatible change to serializers, it's a breaking change to at exactly 1.25:

### Serializing kind/apiVersion breaks on Kubernetes < 1.25
delete_collections returns:
```json
{ status: "Failure", message: "no kind \"DeleteOptions\" is registered for version \"meta.k8s.io/v1\" in scheme \"k8s.io/apimachinery@v1.24.1-k3s1/pkg/runtime/scheme.go:100\"", reason: "", code: 500 }
```
### Not serializing kind/apiVersion breaks on Kubernetes >= 1.25
delete_collection returns:
```json
{ status: "Failure", message: "Object 'Kind' is missing in '{}'", reason: "", code: 500 }
```

So now we have to detect versions in non-IO/protocol level modules to do this safely, and it forces the user on a zero version skew.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/110110: This seems to be the culprit, though I need to do some more investigation to understand the problem.

cc @sxllwx

> #110110: This seems to be the culprit, though I need to do some more investigation to understand the problem.
> 
> cc @sxllwx

Thanks to @Jefftree  for tracking down. It is currently confirmed that this incompatible change is due to [PR-110110](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/110110). The root cause of the problem is being traced.

Update: the problem has been identified, and the specific reasons are as follows:

> The reason for the issue is that the apiserver uses the Scheme in the global variable pkg/api/legacyscheme/scheme.go, and registers the DeleteOptions corresponding to each APIGroup in the Scheme. But DeleteOptions in meta.k8s.io/v1 is not registered, resulting in a notRegisteredErr.

title: Higher kube-apiserver memory usage k8s 1.20.15 vs 1.21.14
body:
### What happened?

After upgrading k8s cluster from 1.20.15 to 1.21.14, we noticed significantly higher memory usage from kube-apiserver pods.

Below are the graphs that show clearly the difference in memory consumption before and after. The spike in the middle is when the control-plane nodes were being rolled to 1.21.

This is a plot of `container_memory_working_set_bytes`.
On 1.20.15 for leader was 5.7Gi, other pods 3Gi.
On 1.21.14 for leader is 9.6Gi, other pods 5.5Gi.
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/89029096/182935427-c1ca78d5-76f3-47c7-85c6-27f9a696f2cb.png)

However, if instead `process_resident_memory_bytes` was plotted, memory usage actually decreased.
On 1.20.15 it was 9.6Gi, on 1.21.14 it is 5.1Gi.
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/89029096/182935628-5cc9a94b-4cf5-4c61-9983-f07f09b3f38e.png)

From my understanding the difference is that `container_memory_working_set_bytes` includes active cache, but the numbers still doesn't quite make sense.
Using `node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes` the control-plane nodes have 5Gi less memory available on 1.21.14, meaning the new 1.21.14 control-plane is using much more memory.

I looked at the k8s 1.21 changelogs and did not find any entries for increased memory usage.
The cluster is quite large at ~100 nodes, with 3 control-plane nodes.

**Questions:**
Is `container_memory_working_set_bytes` an appropriate measure of kube-apiserver memory consumption?
If so, is there an explanation for increased memory usage for kube-apiserver going from 1.20.15 to 1.21.14?

### What did you expect to happen?

No significant change in kube-apiserver memory usage.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Compare `container_memory_working_set_bytes` of kube-apiserver between k8s 1.20 vs 1.21

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

@yuzhouliu9 just wanting to confirm; is your graph specifically `kube-apiserver` or is this just overall usage for a master node running both `kube-apiserver` and `etcd`?

@protosam the graph is a prometheus query of just the `kube-apiserver`:  `container_memory_working_set_bytes{container="kube-apiserver"}`.
The master nodes are running both `kube-apiserver` and `etcd` though.

Both kube-apiserver and etcd can be masters on the same node or be on separate nodes. I'm not sure what these metrics are actually tied to, but you can figure it out by comparing them with `top`.

The relevant columns are going to be:
- `RES` - physical memory footprint without pages and cache
- `USED` - physical memory footprint and swap use without the pages and cache
- `VIRT` - physical memory footprint with pages and cache

1. Shell into a master with  ssh or the kubectl node-shell plugin.
2. Run `top`.
3. Press `shift`+`f` to open up Field Management.
4. Use arrows to highlight `USED`.
5. Press `space` to toggle it (make sure it has a *)
6. With `USED` still highlight, press `s` to sort by it
7. Press `q` to leave Field Management.
8. Press `c` to toggle command args if so desired

---

As for what to consider depends on if kube-apiserver's cache is probably going to depend on if kube-apiserver's memory footprint is heavily influenced by mmap, sockets, and other kernel managed resources.

Normally caches are not relevant for a process and can be ignored. The kernel will just manage it, depending on what it is. This is my default thought process for kube-apiserver unless I learn it does something exceptional. `RES` or `USER` is what I view for this process.

Something exceptional for me is etcd. It uses mmap which obfuscates it's memory impact. `VIRT` is what I observe for this process.

---
Sorry I don't have a clear and concise answer, but hopefully this helps you understand the metric.

Btw, I think release 1.21 is EOL now. These life cycles are crazy short.

Thanks, here are the top 5 processes sorted by `USED`, on a master node.
```
    PID USER      PR  NI    VIRT    RES    SHR S  %CPU  %MEM     TIME+ COMMAND                                                                                                                                                                                           USED

    165 root      19  -1  532.2m 361.9m 360.0m S   0.0   4.7  12:24.47 systemd-journal                                                                                                                                                                                 361.9m
   7261 root      20   0   10.3g 246.6m  44.2m S   2.0   3.2 726:14.30 etcd                                                                                                                                                                                            246.6m
  16593 root      20   0 1153.4m 163.3m  24.9m S   1.0   2.1 485:24.23 ruby
```

With the prometheus query `container_memory_working_set_bytes{container="kube-apiserver"}` the value is 1.43GiB. So not an exact match to `RES` for `kube-apiserver` of 1.2g. I understand memory accounting in Linux is a very complicated subject, so I don't want to really dive into where the difference comes from.

Back to the original topic though. I wasn't looking to understand the metric, but rather inquire why the increased `kube-apiserver` memory usage going from 1.20 to 1.21.

Are you able to share svg's from pprof showing the heaps and allocs? Profiling for kube-apiserver should be enabled by default. 

They can be collected as follows.

Before starting, you need Go and `graphviz` installed to use `go tool pprof`.

Create a loopback context. This hack ensures we will be able to get to the kube-apiserver we desire.
```
kubectl config get-contexts
kubectl config set-cluster local-debugging --server=https://localhost:6443 --insecure-skip-tls-verify=true
kubectl config set-context local-debugging --cluster=local-debugging --user=PUT_AUTHINFO_USER_HERE
```

Start off in your main context. Identify the kube-apiserver pod you want to connect to. Edit the last line to ensure you connect to the right pod name and port.
```
kubectl config use-context REAL_CONTEXT_HERE
kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l k8s-app=kube-apiserver
kubectl -n kube-system port-forward pod/kube-apiserver-ip-100-123-321-33.us-east-5.compute.internal 6443:443
```

With the port-forward running, switch contexts to the debugging context and start a proxy.
```
kubectl config use-context local-debugging
kubectl proxy
```

These commands will host a web based explorer for you to find details in your browser.
```
go tool pprof -http=:6061 http://localhost:8001/debug/pprof/heap
go tool pprof -http=:6061 http://localhost:8001/debug/pprof/allocs
```

This will generate svgs that are easy to use in chrome and easy to share with other people.
```
go tool pprof -svg http://localhost:8001/debug/pprof/heap
mv profile001.svg heap.svg

go tool pprof -svg http://localhost:8001/debug/pprof/allocs
mv profile001.svg allocs.svg
```

If you just want to view the svgs in your browser.
```
go tool pprof -web http://localhost:8001/debug/pprof/heap
go tool pprof -web http://localhost:8001/debug/pprof/allocs
```

See `go tool pprof --help` for more details. There's a lot of stuff it does.

For context, we made these changes to support migration from the legacy cloud provider where --node-ip does have an effect. It was causing a regression moving from legacy cloud provider to external cloud provider to have the behaviour of --node-ip change. I confess I didn't give --node-ip with CCM prior to 1.24 much thought as, other than raise an error if it was invalid, it didn't actually use it at all.

Separately, I wonder if we need to add the ability to support a second node IP via the Node annotation to support dual stack.

Note that this all continues to feel like a stop-gap. I think the intention here was that CCMs would be the canonical source for network configuration information. There are 3 problems with that, though:

* They're not really ready
* They're not actually canonical (the installer is)
* You can't write an automated upgrade if the metadata describing which networks are internal is lost because it was exclusively represented in --node-ip.

The latter problem was the fundamental issue we had in OpenShift. The second is the one is the real architectural problem, although the solution to it will inevitably be custom to each CCM.

The bug here is that we didn't consider that someone might take advantage of the fact that `--node-ip` was broken with external cloud providers and use it only for its side effects...

Oh, I think there's another bug here, which is that if you specify `--node-ip`, then kubelet will annotate the node with `alpha.kubernetes.io/provided-node-ip`, but if you _don't_ specify `--node-ip` (or specify `::` or `0.0.0.0`) then kubelet _doesn't_ remove any existing annotation.

Which means, @chandanD4, I think if you manually remove the `alpha.kubernetes.io/provided-node-ip` annotation from each of your nodes, and then run kubelet 1.24 and cloud-provider 1.24, with `--node-ip ::`, then you will get the behavior that you wanted.
